t.E322.agn: In its 2017 re-evaluation, EFSA saw no need for a numerical acceptable daily intake (ADI) and concluded that there was no safety concern at the reported use levels for people over 1 year of age.
t.E322.body: It is digested like other phospholipids taken in with food; its breakdown products, such as choline, are used in the body's normal metabolism.
t.E322.eff.0.t: If obtained from soya or egg, it may cause an allergic reaction; in the EU its source is declared on the label as an allergen
t.E322.eff.0.w: People with soya or egg allergy
t.E322.eff.1.w: People over 1 year of age without allergies
t.E322.eval: Mostly obtained from soya or sunflower; relevant for people with soya allergy. In the EU, GM soya must be labelled; products from outside the EU may be derived from GM soya.
t.E322.prod: Obtained by physical methods from foods such as soya, sunflower or egg.
t.E322.pw.0: Soya lecithin counts as a soya allergen. If the label says “soya lecithin” or just “lecithin”, the source may be soya.
t.E322.pw.1: Lecithin can also be obtained from egg; in that case egg is declared on the label.
t.E322.pw.2: Egg lecithin is of animal origin; if the source is not stated, you can ask the manufacturer.
t.E322.reg.0: Re-evaluated; a numerical ADI was not considered necessary.
t.E322.reg.1: If derived from soya or egg, it must be declared on the label as an allergen (1169/2011 Annex II).
t.E322.reg.2: In Türkiye, it is on the Turkish Food Codex list of authorised food additives.
t.E322.summary: An emulsifier obtained from soya, sunflower, rapeseed or egg that keeps oil and water mixed.
t.E322.what: It keeps oil and water mixed without separating. It improves the flow of the product and makes it easier to process.
